title: An Antarctic Island Looks Like a Skull, and Its Ice Is Telling a Story
summary:
Seen from above, Vega Island in Antarctica looks like a grinning skull looking toward nearby Devil Island. Behind that spooky sight is a serious story about changing glaciers.

A rocky peak looks like an empty eye socket, a ridge along a glacier outlines the mouth, and a glacier forms the lower jaw.

NASA satellite images, taken by the Operational Land Imager aboard Landsat 9, show the island in March 2025 and again in October 2026. In March 2025, snow covered the land. By October 2026, large sections were free of snow, leaving darker glacier ice exposed.

Glaciologist Mauri Pelto explained that a warm winter in 2026, especially in June, helped cause the exposed ice. Little fresh snow built up, and some snow was lost through sublimation, when ice turns directly into water vapor, and strong winds.

The lack of snow could matter in warmer months. Fresh snow reflects sunlight, while darker ice absorbs more energy and may warm and melt faster. A thin cover of new snow would help in the short run, Pelto said.
why_it_matters: When ice in Antarctica melts faster, it can change sea levels far away, so watching snow cover there matters to everyone.

background_read: A glacier is a huge mass of ice that moves very slowly over land.
Fresh snow is bright and bounces sunlight back, while dark ice soaks up sunlight and warms faster.
Satellites can photograph the same place at different times so scientists can compare snow and ice.
Article_Structure: WHO: Vega Island, its glaciers, and glaciologist Mauri Pelto.
WHAT: Satellite images show far less snow on the island in October 2026 than in March 2025.
WHERE: Vega Island in Antarctica, near Devil Island.
WHY: Warm winter weather left darker ice exposed, which may melt faster.
